title: Reconciling Shopify Payments in QuickBooks Online: The Step-by-Step Workflow
summary: Shopify payouts never match QuickBooks deposits? Learn how to reconcile Shopify in QuickBooks Online in 6 steps: clearing account, fees, refunds and sales tax.
body_markdown:
You made $1,000 in Shopify sales, but only $970 reached your bank account. Where did the other $30 go, and how do you make the numbers match in QuickBooks Online?


It happens because Shopify combines orders into payouts and deducts fees, refunds, and other adjustments before sending the money to your bank. If you record those deposits as sales without accounting for the deductions, your revenue and bank records won’t reconcile.


Actually, it’s a common problem: in Synder’s analysis of 412 retail and ecommerce businesses, 36.4% reported reconciliation issues. And across all 1,033 businesses in the same analysis, 33.6% named fees and payouts confusion as a key challenge.


This guide walks you through how to reconcile Shopify payments in QuickBooks Online in six steps, from setting up a clearing account to matching payouts with bank deposits. You’ll also learn how to handle fees, refunds, and sales tax, troubleshoot discrepancies, and decide whether manual reconciliation or automation makes more sense for your business.


## **TL;DR: how to reconcile Shopify in QuickBooks in 6 steps**


1. Sync every Shopify sale, fee, and refund into a Shopify clearing account in QuickBooks Online.
2. If you use the native connector, confirm the imported transactions so they post to your books.
3. Open the Shopify payout detail and note the payout ID.
4. Match the net payout to its bank deposit in QuickBooks, using Match, never Add.
5. Reconcile the bank account, then compare QuickBooks revenue with Shopify net sales.
6. Check that each sent payout nets to zero in the clearing account, and list payouts still on their way to your bank as deposits in transit.


## **Why a Shopify payout does not match QuickBooks**


A Shopify payout is a net amount, so it won’t equal the sales total Shopify shows for the same days. To make the two match, QuickBooks needs both the gross sales and each deduction behind the deposit. If you record the deposit as revenue instead, you’ll understate sales, miss processing expenses, and make reconciliation harder.


### **Where the gap comes from**


Each payout covers sales from one or more days, minus refunds, fees, and sometimes chargebacks.


Sales tax is handled differently: Shopify usually doesn’t withhold it, and it arrives in your payout even though you owe it to the tax authority. The exception is when Shopify collects and remits tax for you, for example as a marketplace facilitator or for import tax on cross-border orders. That tax never reaches your payout, but it still needs to appear in your books.


To see how these deductions add up, here’s how a $50,000 week of Shopify sales becomes a $47,800 deposit:


**Component** **Example amount** **QuickBooks account**


Gross product sales Included in $50,000 Shopify Sales (income)


Discounts Included in $50,000 (net) Discounts (contra-revenue)


Shipping charged Included in $50,000 Shipping Income


Sales tax collected Included in $50,000 Sales Tax Payable (liability)


**Total collected from customers** **$50,000** Shopify Payments Clearing


Refunds −$400 Refunds & Returns (contra-revenue)


Processing fees −$1,800 Shopify Fees (expense)


Chargeback + $15 fee $0 this week Chargebacks (expense)


Reserve hold $0 this week Stays in clearing until released


Other adjustments $0 this week Depends on the adjustment


**Net payout = bank deposit** **$47,800** Checking


**Clearing balance after payout** **$0.00** Shopify Payments Clearing


Two deductions in that table need a closer look: chargebacks and reserves. According to[Shopify’s chargeback guide](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/payments/chargebacks/chargeback-process) , a US Shopify Payments chargeback removes the disputed amount and a $15 fee from your balance right away, and you get the fee back if you win the dispute. Shopify may also hold part of your balance in a reserve to cover future disputes and refunds, so that money reaches you later.


### **How payout timing creates gaps**


Timing adds another complication, since Shopify may pay out every few days, Amazon typically settles on a two-week cycle, and PayPal follows its own schedule. A sale recorded in June might reach your bank in July, leaving a balance to account for when closing June’s books.


Refunds make these gaps wider, because a refund you issue today comes out of a later payout. The sale and the refund can end up in different accounting periods, and across hundreds of orders, those small gaps add up.


*If you haven’t connected Shopify to QuickBooks yet, read our guide on*[how to import Shopify sales into QuickBooks Online](https://synder.com/blog/how-to-bring-shopify-transactions-into-quickbooks-with-synder/) *.*


### **When a payout crosses month-end**


If a payout leaves Shopify in one month and reaches your bank in the next, it’s a timing difference, not a mistake. The payout is recorded on the date Shopify sends it, so the clearing account still clears that month, and the money on its way shows up as a deposit in transit in your bank reconciliation.


Your[Shopify payout schedule](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/payments/shopify-payments/payouts) (daily, weekly, or monthly) doesn’t follow your accounting month, and according to[Shopify’s payout timing page](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/payments/shopify-payments/payouts/payout-timing) , a sent payout can take another 1–3 days to reach your bank, so this can happen at any month-end.


When the dates cross over, use these steps to reconcile Shopify payouts in QuickBooks:


1. **List the payouts in transit.** On the last day of the month, write down every payout Shopify has sent that hasn’t reached your bank yet.
2. **Record them on the payout date.** Post each one as a transfer from the clearing account to your bank on the date Shopify sent it, or let an integration tool like[Synder](https://synder.com/) do this automatically.
3. **Mark them as deposits in transit.** When you reconcile your bank account, leave these payouts uncleared and note their payout IDs, so anyone reviewing the close can see why the bank statement is lower.
4. **Confirm they clear next month.** In the first days of the new month, check that each listed payout has been matched to a deposit.


A clearing account is a type of account that acts as a placeholder. The money flows to this account after the activity in Shopify gets posted, and then flows out when the actual payment is received by the bank. A clearing account helps to match all transactions with Shopify individually against one bulk payment with QuickBooks. Workflow is important in the correct sequence, since posting transactions before matching will prevent double posting of revenues, which is probably the most frequent mistake.


## **How the Shopify clearing account works in QuickBooks Online**


A clearing account is a holding account between Shopify and your bank. It’s what makes Shopify payouts reconciliation in QuickBooks possible, because it separates what you sold from what you received. Each sale goes into the account at its full amount. When Shopify sends the payout, the payout and its fees come out, so the account goes back to zero.


Your target is a clearing balance that matches what Shopify is still holding, which drops to zero once every sale has been paid out. Money that’s still on its way to your bank doesn’t belong here, because it appears as a deposit in transit in your bank reconciliation. Any other difference means a fee, refund, or adjustment was missed or posted to the wrong account.


### **How to create a Shopify clearing account in QuickBooks Online**


Each gateway pays out separately, so create one clearing account for each one, a setup that takes a couple of minutes:


1. **Go to Accounting → Chart of accounts and click New.**
2. **Set the account type to Bank.**
3. **Name the account after the gateway** , for example “Shopify Payments Clearing” or “PayPal Clearing.”
4. **Use the same names in every client file** , since consistent names make month-end reviews and handoffs faster.


Once the account exists, you match each Shopify Payments payout in the bank feed. A deposit from another processor, like PayPal, is handled differently, because you record it as a transfer out of that processor’s clearing account.


To see how it works, here’s how one order on the Shopify Basic plan moves through the account. The customer pays $108 ($100 for the product plus $8 sales tax), Shopify charges a $3.43 fee (2.9% + 30¢), and you receive $104.57.


**Entry** **Debit** **Credit**


Sale Shopify Payments Clearing $108.00 Shopify Sales $100.00; Sales Tax Payable $8.00


Payout Checking $104.57; Shopify Fees $3.43 Shopify Payments Clearing $108.00


As a result, the account goes up by $108 and back down by $108, leaving a zero balance.


QuickBooks’ own Shopify connector skips the clearing account and holds Shopify money in Undeposited Funds (shown as “Payments to Deposit”), creating a bank deposit when you confirm a payout. Because Undeposited Funds also holds checks and other customer payments, your Shopify money gets mixed in with everything else. A separate clearing account avoids that by keeping Shopify money on its own line.


**For accounting firms:** Use the same naming pattern, such as “\[Gateway\] Clearing,” for every client, and test the setup for a month before you switch a new client to automated sync.[Prince Edward Island Preserve Company](https://synder.com/success-stories/prince-edward-island-preserve-company/) took this approach, using Synder in parallel with its existing processes and comparing a day’s worth of transactions at a time before going live.


Accounting firm[Decimal](https://synder.com/success-stories/decimal/) shows what that switch can deliver: after moving its Shopify, Stripe, PayPal, and Amazon clients to automated sync and reconciliation, the firm saves 6–8 hours per client each month. Kristin Miller, Team Lead at Decimal, said:


> Synder’s automatic categorization feature has been invaluable for clients managing high transaction volumes and complex reporting needs.
>
>
> Kristin Miller, Team Lead at Decimal


### **Keep one clearing account per payment gateway**


Each gateway, like PayPal or Klarna, sends money on its own schedule and terms. If they all share one clearing account, the balance won’t clear to zero, and you won’t be able to tell which gateway caused the gap.


PayPal is a frequent second gateway, appearing in 34.5% of the retail businesses in Synder’s internal data, so it’s worth setting up correctly. To keep PayPal and Shopify Payments apart:


1. Post PayPal sales to PayPal Clearing, not to Shopify Payments Clearing.
2. Record PayPal fees from your PayPal statement, because they don’t appear in the Shopify payout.
3. When PayPal’s transfer reaches your bank, record it as a transfer out of PayPal Clearing and match it in the bank feed.


[Healthy Meals Direct](https://synder.com/success-stories/healthy-meals-direct/) , which sells through Shopify and PayPal, follows this setup with automated sync. Its Shopify transaction fees and PayPal processing fees are categorized separately, so each clearing account empties on its own.


Shop Pay Installments, however, can share the Shopify Payments clearing account with your card sales. According to[Shopify’s Installments payout guide](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/payments/shop-pay-installments/getting-paid) , Installments money arrives in the same payout as your card sales and follows the same schedule, and you can filter the payout by payment method to see Installments on their own. If you use a custom payout schedule,[Shopify notes](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/payments/shop-pay-installments/faq) that it doesn’t apply to Installments, so those payouts may arrive at different times.


## **How to categorize Shopify in QuickBooks: set up your chart of accounts first**


Before you import or match anything, set up the right accounts, because if sales, fees, refunds, and taxes all post to the same place, your revenue will be wrong and reconciliation won’t add up.


Most stores need at least the accounts below, and the last column shows which Shopify transactions post to each one:


**Account** **QuickBooks type / detail type** **What posts there**


Shopify Sales Income / Sales of Product Income Sales


Shipping Income Income / Service/Fee Income Shipping charged on orders


Discounts Income (contra) / Discounts/Refunds Given Discount codes and automatic discounts


Refunds & Returns Income (contra) / Discounts/Refunds Given Refunds


Shopify Fees Expense / Bank Charges Processing and currency conversion fees, plus third-party transaction fees (billed on your Shopify invoice)


Shipping Labels Expense Shipping labels bought in Shopify


Chargebacks Expense / Other Miscellaneous Service Cost Chargebacks, chargeback fees, and reversals


Sales Tax Payable Other Current Liabilities / Sales Tax Payable Sales tax collected (QuickBooks creates this account when you turn on sales tax)


Gift Card Liability Other Current Liabilities / Other Current Liabilities Gift cards sold (credit) and redeemed (debit)


Shopify Payments Clearing Bank Sales in; refunds, fees, chargebacks, and payouts out


Gift cards need extra care, because an unredeemed gift card is a liability. You record the revenue only when the customer uses it.


## **How to reconcile Shopify payments in QuickBooks Online, step by step**


The order of these steps matters, because posting transactions before you match deposits keeps you from counting the same revenue twice.


Here’s how to reconcile Shopify sales in QuickBooks, whether you use Intuit’s Shopify Connector by QuickBooks or an integration tool like Synder:


1. **Sync your Shopify sales activity.** With Intuit’s Shopify Connector by QuickBooks, imported sales, refunds, fees, and payouts appear in All apps → Accounting → Integration transactions (some screens still call it App transactions). Each confirmed sale posts as a sales receipt at the order total, with fees as a separate expense, to Undeposited Funds (Payments to Deposit). With Synder, sales, refunds, and fees post to a Shopify clearing account, and payouts post as transfers to checking.
2. **Confirm the transactions (native connector only).** In Integration transactions, check that customers, products, and accounts are correct before you confirm them, because unconfirmed transactions don’t appear in your reports and confirmed ones move to the Categorized tab. Synder users can skip this step: synced transactions are already in your books.
3. **Open the payout details in Shopify.** Go to Finance → Payouts in your Shopify admin and select the payout to see its charges, refunds, fees, and adjustments. Copy the payout ID into the QuickBooks memo, or attach the exported payout CSV, so you can trace every entry back to Shopify.
4. **Match the payout to the bank deposit.** Go to All apps → Accounting → Bank transactions, open the For review tab, find the Shopify deposit, and choose Match, not Add.[Intuit’s guidance](https://quickbooks.intuit.com/learn-support/en-us/help-article/manage-integrations/connect-shopify-quickbooks-online/L1Xv7ZCFB_US_en_US) reads: “Do not manually Add the deposit in the bank feed. Always use Match.” With the native connector, confirm the payout in Integration transactions first, so there’s a deposit to match.
5. **Reconcile the bank account, then the P&L.** Reconcile your checking account each month and compare QuickBooks income with Total sales minus Taxes in Shopify’s Finance Summary (Analytics → Reports → Finance Summary) for the same dates. Skip net sales for this check, because it leaves out shipping. Small differences can still appear from gift cards, marketplace-withheld tax, or Shopify reporting sales by order date.
6. **Check the clearing account.** Open the Shopify Payments Clearing register and make sure each payout Shopify has sent nets to zero against its sales, refunds, and fees. Whatever balance remains should match what Shopify is still holding, such as pending payouts and reserves, so it won’t always be $0.00. Payouts already recorded but not yet in your bank show up as deposits in transit in your bank reconciliation. ****


If you record payouts by hand, split the deposit in step 4 into the gross amount from the clearing account and a negative line for Shopify fees. With the native connector, follow Intuit’s order: confirm the transactions, add the payout, then match it in the bank feed.


*For setup tips, see our guide to*[setting up your Shopify QuickBooks integration](https://synder.com/blog/shopify-quickbooks-online-integration/) *.*


[Healthy Meals Direct](https://synder.com/success-stories/healthy-meals-direct/) , a Long Island meal prep service, follows a similar workflow. Before automating, the team spent three to four hours a day on manual reconciliation because of unallocated sales tax and scattered data. With Synder’s Per Transaction Sync, that dropped to 30–45 minutes a day, saving more than 70 hours a month across 100,000+ transactions and 30+ locations.


### **How to record Shopify sales in QuickBooks Online**


There are three ways to enter Shopify sales into QuickBooks, and the right one depends on how many orders you process:


- **A sales receipt for each order** gives you the most detail but takes the most work, so it suits stores with a handful of orders a day.
- **One summary journal entry per payout** , or a daily sales summary, cuts your entries down to one per payout and suits steady volume you reconcile by hand.
- **A connector or app** , such as the native Shopify Connector or a third-party tool, posts the entries for you and makes sense once you process more than a few dozen orders a day or use more than one gateway.


*For a full walkthrough, see*[how to bring Shopify transactions into QuickBooks with Synder](https://synder.com/blog/how-to-bring-shopify-transactions-into-quickbooks-with-synder/) *.*


### **Why your Shopify clearing account isn’t zero (and how to fix it)**


A clearing balance that doesn’t match what Shopify is still holding means something between Shopify and your bank wasn’t recorded, matched, or mapped correctly. It can also explain why Shopify orders and accounting do not reconcile at month-end.


A leftover balance is more than a bookkeeping detail, because if your clearing account shows $18,000 on June 30, that’s $18,000 in sales recorded as revenue that never went through bank reconciliation. The table below matches what you see to its likely cause and fix.


**What you see** **Likely cause** **How to fix it**


Balance equals one or two recent payouts Payout transfer not recorded, or dated when the money arrived Record the transfer on the Shopify payout date (see “When a payout crosses month-end”)


Balance equals a small, odd amount Unposted fee Post the fee from the payout detail to Shopify Fees


Balance is negative or off by one order Refund deducted from a later payout Post the refund against the payout it came out of


Payout short by an order value + $15 Chargeback Record the disputed amount and fee in Chargebacks


Payout smaller than expected, no refund or fee Reserve hold Leave it in clearing until Shopify releases the funds


Off by a few cents or dollars on foreign orders Multi-currency conversion Post the difference to Shopify Fees


PayPal amounts in Shopify clearing Another gateway posting to the wrong account Move them to PayPal Clearing


Revenue appears twice, clearing stays high Deposit added instead of matched (duplicate) Delete the extra deposit (see “The native Shopify Connector by QuickBooks”)


If none of these fits, work backward from the payout detail report, the most useful Shopify reconciliation report for this. Compare each payout’s lines with the clearing account register until you find the missing one.


## **Catch-up reconciliation for a new Shopify client**


To catch up a new Shopify client with messy books, start from a clean date and reconcile one payout at a time, beginning with the oldest open month. Avoid clearing the backlog with one large plug journal entry, because it hides errors instead of fixing them.


This comes up more often than you might expect, since 21.8% of retail businesses in Synder’s internal research were also dealing with a historical cleanup when they started automating.


Say you take on a client in April whose Shopify deposits have been booked as revenue since last year. Work through the open period in this order:


1. **Choose a start date.** This is usually the first day after the last period that was reconciled and filed. Lock the books at that date in QuickBooks Online (Settings → Account and settings → Advanced → Close the books).
2. **Recode the deposits.** From the start date forward, move Shopify deposits out of revenue, so they’re free to match against payouts.
3. **Set the opening clearing balance.** Use the Shopify Payments balance on the start date, which Shopify shows as your next payout plus any reserved funds, already net of fees, refunds, and chargebacks. Payouts Shopify had already sent but your bank hadn’t received are deposits in transit, not clearing.
4. **Import transactions from the start date forward.** QuickBooks’ own connector imports up to one year of history. Synder sets no depth limit of its own, although imports count toward your plan’s sync limit and trials cover one month.
5. **Reconcile payout by payout.** Start with the oldest open month and match each deposit to its payout before you move on.
6. **Clear leftover differences with documented adjusting entries,** one month at a time. Each entry should name the payout or order it corrects.


Synder cleared a similar backlog for[Betr Health](https://synder.com/success-stories/betr-health/) by importing its historical transactions from several ecommerce platforms, dating back to 2020, into QuickBooks Online, so the team could reconcile in real time from then on.


## **Proper handling of Shopify fees, refunds, and sales tax**


Fees and refunds come out of your payout, while sales tax usually comes in with it, and each of them needs its own account in QuickBooks.


### **How to categorize Shopify fees in QuickBooks**


Map Shopify fees to a dedicated expense account so your revenue and costs both stay accurate. Fees aren’t always easy to spot in an export, so here’s what to look for:


**Fee type** **Where it comes from** **QuickBooks account**


Card processing fee Deducted from each Shopify Payments payout (Basic plan, US online: 2.9% + 30¢) Shopify Fees


Third-party transaction fee Charged on your Shopify invoice when you don’t use Shopify Payments (Basic plan: 2%) Shopify Fees


Chargeback fee Withdrawn from your balance with the disputed amount when a chargeback is filed ($15 in the US), and returned if you win Chargebacks


Currency conversion fee Charged when a customer pays in a different currency from your payout (1.5% for US stores) Shopify Fees


These rates come from[Shopify’s US pricing page](https://www.shopify.com/pricing) as of November 2026, and higher plans pay lower card and third-party rates. Subscription and app charges usually appear on your Shopify bill, not in your payout, so record them as regular expenses. Some other charges do come out of your payout, including[Shopify Capital](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/finance/shopify-capital/united-states) repayments,[Shopify Credit](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/finance/shopify-credit/manage-account) repayments from sales, and[Managed Markets](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/international/managed-markets/shopify-payments) fees, duties, and shipping labels.


### **Recording refunds and chargebacks**


Record refunds in a separate refunds and returns account so your sales and returns stay visible, and watch for two situations in particular:


- **Refunds on a later payout.** If you issue a refund after the original payout, Shopify deducts it from a later one. When refunds in a batch are larger than sales, the payout is negative, and QuickBooks’ native connector records it to a separate “Payments account.”
- **Chargebacks.** The disputed amount and the $15 fee (in the US) leave your balance right away. If you win the dispute, both come back on a later payout, so record the reversal in the same Chargebacks account.


### **How to reconcile Shopify sales tax in QuickBooks**


Sales tax you collect belongs in Sales Tax Payable, not in income, because you owe it to the tax authority. It shows up in the Shopify Finance Summary, but it shouldn’t appear on your P&L.


To keep the two in line, check once a month that the Shopify tax report by jurisdiction matches the change in Sales Tax Payable. If QuickBooks Automated Sales Tax is on, QuickBooks calculates tax by location. If it’s off, the native connector posts tax to a default “Shopify Sales Tax Item,” which you’ll need to split by jurisdiction yourself.


This check matters most if you sell in several states. Healthy Meals Direct, for example, needed sales tax broken out for New York’s monthly Prompt Tax filing, and automated tax categorization solved it.


*For more on how Shopify handles tax, read our guide to*[Shopify sales tax](https://synder.com/blog/does-shopify-collect-sales-tax/) *.*


## **Three ways to reconcile QuickBooks and Shopify**


If you’re deciding which approach fits your store, you have three options. The right one depends on your order volume, how many payment gateways you use, and how much time you can give to bookkeeping.


### **Manual reconciliation**


With manual reconciliation, you record Shopify activity yourself, map fees, refunds, and taxes, and match each payout through a clearing account. It costs nothing but your time and gives you full control. The downside is that it slows down as volume grows, because you have to review every payout separately.


### **The native Shopify Connector by QuickBooks**


Intuit’s Shopify Connector by QuickBooks imports your Shopify sales, refunds, fees, and payouts into QuickBooks Online. By default, you review and confirm them before they post, but if you turn on Add transactions automatically, QuickBooks posts high-confidence transactions for you. The connector is free to install, and you need a QuickBooks Online subscription and a Shopify account to use it.[Intuit’s help article](https://quickbooks.intuit.com/learn-support/en-us/help-article/manage-integrations/connect-shopify-quickbooks-online/L1Xv7ZCFB_US_en_US) explains the setup step by step, so here’s a quick look at what the connector does well and where you’ll still need to step in:


**Handles well** **Where you’ll still work by hand**


Imports Shopify sales, refunds, fees, and payouts into App transactions Choosing an account for some payout adjustments


Imports up to one year of history Separate clearing per gateway (it uses Undeposited Funds instead)


Keeps transactions out of reports until you confirm them, unless Add transactions automatically is on Sales tax by jurisdiction when Automated Sales Tax is off


Creates a bank deposit when you confirm a payout Negative payouts, which go to a separate Payments account


B2B invoices and extra monthly journal entries


Duplicate deposits are the most common native-connector error, and they’re easy to fix:


- **Why it happens:** someone added the deposit in the bank feed after the connector had already posted the payout.
- **How to fix it:** find the second deposit in the bank register, delete it, and keep the matched payout.
- **How to prevent it:** confirm App transactions first, then match the deposit without adding it manually.

### **Shopify cash reconciliation best practices: a month-end checklist**


Before you close the month, go through these checks, which cover what the six steps don’t:


- Your clearing account balance matches what Shopify is still holding (pending payouts and reserves), and payouts still on their way to your bank are listed as deposits in transit, with payout IDs.
- The change in Sales Tax Payable equals the Shopify tax report for the month.
- Income on your P&L equals Total sales minus Taxes in Shopify’s Finance Summary.
- You’ve checked next month’s first bank deposits, so you can confirm the deposits in transit cleared.


## **How to choose the right approach**


A few questions can help you pick the right method:


- **How many orders do you process?** A few transactions a day are manageable by hand, but hundreds or thousands a month make automation worth the cost.
- **How many gateways do you use?** One payment processor is easy to handle with a connector. Once you add PayPal or Stripe alongside Shopify, a third-party integration keeps the mapping accurate.
- **How much detail do you need?** If you track items or cost of goods sold (COGS) closely, Per Transaction Sync gives you that detail, while Summary Sync keeps your books simpler.
- **How complex are your taxes?** Selling in several states or issuing B2B invoices makes automated tax mapping much more useful.
- **Have you tested it?** Setup and pricing don’t suit everyone, so use a free trial to confirm a tool fits your workflow.


### **Per Transaction vs Summary Sync: which is better for Shopify reconciliation?**


The right sync mode depends on how much detail you want in QuickBooks:


**Per Transaction Sync** **Summary Sync**


What posts Every sale, refund, and fee as its own record One summary per day or payout

Based on Synder’s internal data from March–August 2026, retail and ecommerce finance teams pick Summary Sync far more often than other users do: 40% of in-house finance users and 43% of outsourced accountants chose daily Summary Sync when they signed up, compared with 26% of all signups.


- **In-house controllers:** choose Per Transaction Sync if you report margins by product, and Summary Sync otherwise, since it keeps your close faster.
- **Bookkeepers with several Shopify clients:** start with Summary Sync for consistency, and switch a client to Per Transaction Sync when they need SKU-level reporting.
- **Growing brand owners:** start with Summary Sync and switch when you need product-level profit reports.


## **Final thoughts**


The key to Shopify QuickBooks reconciliation is remembering that a deposit isn’t a sale. So record each part of a payout in its own account, match payouts through a clearing account, and use the month-end checklist above before you close each period.


## **FAQ**


### **How do I allocate my Shopify payout in QuickBooks?**


To allocate a Shopify payout in QuickBooks, split the net amount into its parts. Gross sales go to revenue, fees to your fees expense account, refunds to your returns account, and chargebacks and adjustments to their own accounts. Then match the bank deposit to the payout so the amount moves from the clearing account to checking. The table in “Where the gap comes from” shows where each part goes.


### **How often should I reconcile Shopify in QuickBooks Online?**


Reconcile Shopify in QuickBooks Online at least once a month, and after every payout if you have a high-volume store. Checking daily or weekly helps you catch discrepancies early, and automation makes that practical without extra manual work. If a payout crosses into the next month, follow the month-end steps above.


### **Which QuickBooks works with Shopify?**


QuickBooks Online integrates with Shopify, both through Intuit’s native Shopify Connector app and through third-party tools. QuickBooks Desktop has more limited options. Most ecommerce sellers use QuickBooks Online because it supports app-based syncing, bank feed matching, and the clearing-account workflows that Shopify reconciliation depends on.


### **Why doesn’t my Shopify clearing account return to zero?**


A non-zero clearing account almost always means something is unrecorded: a fee that wasn’t booked, a refund stranded on a different payout, a pending or multi-currency transaction, or a payout you haven’t matched yet. Work backward from the Shopify payout report to find the missing piece, then post the adjustment so the account clears.
